objects.title: Hydrometer (third from left in photo)
objects.imageAlt: Museum image for Hydrometer (third from left in photo)
objects.description: This hydrometer’s (third from left in photo) glass bulb is anchored with lead shot at its lower end. The instrument contains a U.S. Internal Revenue tax stamp C4205, which features an engraving of George Washington, the same image found on the U.S. one dollar bill. The engraved stamp was inserted into the bulb during manufacture by an agent of the Commissioner of Internal Revenue as authoritative proof of the scale’s accuracy. The number C4205 indicates the stamp was delivered to the Internal Revenue Bureau from the Bureau of Engraving and Printing on January 23, 1905. An accurate scale was essential for determining the alcohol content of wine for tax purposes.

objects.title: Book, "The Life of George Washington", 1813
objects.imageAlt: Museum image for Book, "The Life of George Washington", 1813
objects.description: Mason Locke Weems’s biography of George Washington became the most widely read 19th century book about the Revolutionary War and its celebrated hero. Weems recounted many familiar anecdotes about Washington, including the famous story of the cherry tree, and helped to establish a national narrative that cemented Founding Fathers in our national consciousness. Washington’s stature as Father of our Country is borne out by the dozens of pageants and plays that celebrated the bicentennial of his birth and continue today.

objects.title: Campaign Lantern
objects.imageAlt: Museum image for Campaign Lantern
objects.description: Political campaigns of the 19th century reflected popular traditions of commemoration and celebration—such as Fourth of July parades—that became familiar to many Americans in the early Republic. The mechanisms of popular politics not specifically called for in the Constitution—parties, nominating conventions, and electoral campaigns—drew freely on the evocative imagery of such festivities in promoting candidates and building the momentum of the campaign. Mass campaign spectacles arose as a way of demonstrating partisan strength and of mobilizing indifferent and easily distracted voters. The successful presidential campaign of Republican Abraham Lincoln perfected the nighttime torchlight parade in which marchers torches and lanterns, such as this one displaying an American eagle, created a sometimes provocative spectacle.

objects.title: Commemorative Clothing Button, George Washington, 1789
objects.imageAlt: Photograph of “Long Live the President GW” Button
objects.description: Buttons such as this one reading “Long Live the President GW” were worn by supporters of George Washington during his first inauguration. There was no formal campaigning process during the first election. The framers of the Constitution presumed that the highly esteemed Washington would serve as the country’s first president, and he was elected unanimously by the Electoral College, with John Adams being elected as his vice president. There were no political parties at the time of Washington’s election, and though the Federalist and Democratic-Republican parties began forming during his time in office, he remained officially non-partisan.
objects.story: A big day arrives: Washington becomes the first U.S. president. People celebrate by wearing little brass buttons like this one. Can you see the letters GW?

objects.title: Decanter, Zachary Taylor, 1848
objects.imageAlt: Museum image for Decanter, Zachary Taylor, 1848
objects.description: This glass decanter marks Zachary Taylor’s successful run for president in 1848, as a Whig, against Democrat Lewis Cass and Free Soil Party Candidate Martin Van Buren. Taylor rode his successful generalship in the recent war in Mexico, and his promise to put his allegiance to the country above partisanship, to the White House. This decanter was probably used for wine and spirits, but it was ultimately a glass of milk and some cherries which did him in, causing an unknown digestive ailment which killed him, after a little more than a year in the White House.

objects.title: Know Nothing Poster, 1854
objects.imageAlt: Museum image for Know Nothing Poster, 1854
objects.description: The American Party, also called the Know-Nothings, was a major national political force in the 1850s. It saw immigrants and Catholics as the greatest threat to self-government and to the nation. Arguing for rule by native-born Protestants, the Know-Nothings ran former President Millard Fillmore as their presidential candidate in the 1856 election. Though James Buchanan won the presidency, Fillmore received over 21 percent of the vote. During the Civil War the movement fractured and largely disappeared, but fear and distrust of new immigrants remained within the core beliefs of many future political movements. This 1850s advertising broadside is for The Dollar Weekly Times, an American Party-affiliated newspaper.

objects.title: Paperweight, Herbert Hoover, 1928
objects.imageAlt: Museum image for Paperweight, Herbert Hoover, 1928
objects.description: This iron paperweight is designed to look like a pile of 29 coins each of which is stamped with the inauguration year of one of the presidents of the United States. The top coin features both George Washington and Herbert Hoover, the 1928 Republican presidential nominee. The pile seems to be one coin short because when Hoover won he became the 31st president. But it was not a mistake; Grover Cleveland was given just one coin in the pile to represent his two non-consecutive terms in office.

objects.title: Pitcher, "Union to the People"
objects.imageAlt: Museum image for Pitcher, "Union to the People"
objects.description: This transfer printed creamware pitcher is decorated with a maritime print on one side and a print celebrating the new Liberty of the United States on the other side. The maritime design shows a ship under sail. The other side shows three men, likely George Washington, John Adams and Thomas Jefferson, clasping hands and holding a liberty pole. A scroll above reads “Union to the People of America” and beneath “Civil and Religious Liberty to all Mankind.”

objects.title: Pitcher, "An Emblem of America"
objects.imageAlt: Museum image for Pitcher, "An Emblem of America"
objects.description: This transfer printed creamware pitcher was made by Herculaneum Pottery in Liverpool, England around 1800. On the front is a print of the Cooper’s Guild Coat of Arms with the motto “Prosperity attend the integrity of our cause” below on a banner. On the reverse is the print titled “An Emblem for America.” It depicts the allegorical figure of Columbia holding a flag and showing two dark skinned Native Americans (who served as iconography for the Western Hemisphere). To Columbia’s left are portraits of men involved in the discovery of North America and the founding of the United States: Christopher Columbus, “Americus” Vespucci, Sir Walter Raleigh, George Washington, Benjamin Franklin, and John Adams. Under the spout is a print declaring “Peace and Commerce” an images of the all-seeing eye, the French and American flags knotted, and two hands clasped in a handshake. Just above are the initials “JS.” The print “An Emblem for America” is based on an engraving in a series by John Fairburn of London. Robert H. McCauley purchased this jug from the Boston Antique Shop of Boston, MA on December 30, 1938 for $75.00.

objects.title: Prang Lithographic School Room Portrait of George Washington by Gilbert Stuart
objects.displayTitle: Prang Lithographic School Room Portrait of George Washington by Gilbert Stuart
objects.imageAlt: Museum image for Prang Lithographic School Room Portrait of George Washington by Gilbert Stuart
objects.description: This lithograph, copied from a Gilbert Stuart portrait of George Washington, was commercially sold in school catalogs and for homes, libraries, and public buildings across America. Images of “the father of our country” became familiar instructional tools as well as a school decoration and patriotic imagery. The print was mass produced in 1901 by Taber Prang Art Company, founded by Louis Prang. Louis Prang also founded the Prang Educational Company to develop artistic abilities in school age children. The print continued to be reproduced by Prang until 1938.

objects.title: George Washington's Dispatch Case
objects.imageAlt: Museum image for George Washington's Dispatch Case
objects.description: George Washington's traveling dispatch case, used while he was the commander-in-chief of the Continental Army during the Revolutionary War. The case is a slight rectangular box made of mahogany and covered with black leather. A hinged lid at the bottom opens to reveal several compartments for writing implements while the top has a leather pocket for stationary and documents. It could easily be slipped into a saddle or travel bag and carried to its owner’s next location.

objects.title: The Resignation of Pres. Washington
topics: In Pursuit of Life, Liberty, and Happiness
objects.imageAlt: Museum image for The Resignation of Pres. Washington
objects.description: In September 1796, George Washington announced he would not seek a third term as the nation’s first president. His statement has come to be known as Washington’s Farewell Address although he did not deliver it as public speech. He wrote it as a letter under the simple heading “To the People of the United States.” Over 7000 words long, Washington’s Farewell was published across the country first in newspapers and later in small books.

topics: In Pursuit of Life, Liberty, and Happiness
objects.imageAlt: Museum image for Finger bowl from George and Martha Washington's formal dinner service
objects.description: This finger bowl was likely used for entertaining in the presidential mansion in Philadelphia and later at Mount Vernon. When Washington resigned the presidency and retired to Mount Vernon, he took with him the china, glassware, and furnishings that he had personally supplied for the presidential mansion. He noted that that, at his own expense, he had frequently needed to replace glassware that was broken in the presidential mansion.

He noted that that, at his own expense, he had frequently needed to replace glassware that was broken in the presidential mansion.

objects.title: Braddock Pistol
objectType: Firearms; Flintlock; .71 In; Muzzle Load; 00; Sa
objects.imageAlt: Photograph of Braddock Pistol Used by Washington
objects.description: Physical Description
objects.story: A British general gave Washington this pistol. Washington carried it on later army trips. Now the museum keeps it safe so we can learn its story.

objects.title: Breeches worn by General George Washington
objects.displayTitle: Breeches worn by General George Washington
objects.imageAlt: Photograph of Washington’s Buff Wool Breeches
objects.description: Buff wool breeches worn by George Washington. Breeches have a two-button closure at waist and a waistband which is lined with linen. The front flap has a one-button closure on either side. There are two front pockets, with a watch pocket on the proper right side of the waistband. The legs have a five-button closure, with a separate tab and button on leg openings. Although presented through the years as a uniform consisting of coat, waistcoat and breeches, the waistcoat and breeches are actually from an earlier uniform dating from the end of the Revolutionary War. The coat is slightly newer, dating from 1789.
objects.story: Washington’s outfit needs pants, too. These wool breeches stop near the knees. Clothes looked a little different long ago.

objects.title: camp cup
objects.imageAlt: Museum image for camp cup
objects.description: The Smithsonian catalog connects this object to George Washington.
objects.story: Look closely at this object and consider how the Smithsonian connects it to George Washington.

objects.title: George Washington's Battle Sword and Scabbard
objects.displayTitle: George Washington's Battle Sword and Scabbard
objects.imageAlt: Photograph of George Washington's Battle Sword and Scabbard
objects.description: Physical Description
objects.story: Here is the steel sword Washington wore while leading his army. It traveled with him during the Revolutionary War. Look for the long metal blade.

objects.title: George Washington's Camp Chest
objectType: mess kit; camp chest; Equipment, Individual
objects.imageAlt: Photograph of George Washington's Camp Chest
objects.description: Armies on campaign must carry with them much besides their weapons. At the time of the American Revolutionary War (1776-1781), various boxes and chests transported soldier's individual effects, wardrobes, official military payrolls, and other necessities. Camp chests or canteens as they were called in the 18th century, carried utensils and cooking apparatus to be used by officers and their staff when in the field during campaigns.
objects.story: Imagine the army getting ready to move. Washington brings this camp chest along. Inside are things he needs for cooking and eating on the journey.

objects.title: George Washington's Camp Stool
objects.imageAlt: Photograph of George Washington’s Camp Stool
objects.description: Physical Description
objects.story: It is time for a rest at camp. Washington can unfold this small stool and sit down. Then it folds up again for the next trip.

objects.title: George Washington's Epaulettes
objectType: Epaulets, pair of; Insignia; Army; Holder, Epaulet; Officer
objects.imageAlt: Photograph of George Washington's Epaulettes
objects.description: Physical Description
objects.story: Something shiny rests on Washington’s shoulders. These gold pieces are called epaulettes. Artists put them in paintings of him, too.

objects.title: George Washington's Uniform
objectType: coat; Man; Army; General Officer; Officer
topics: In Pursuit of Life, Liberty, and Happiness
objects.imageAlt: Photograph of George Washington's Uniform
objects.description: This uniform consisting of coat, waistcoat, and knee breeches was worn by George Washington from 1789 until his death in 1799. The "small clothes," or breeches and waistcoat, date from the revolutionary period. The coat dates to 1789.
objects.story: Washington gets dressed in his blue and tan army coat. People can spot their leader by the clothes he wears. Can you find both colors?

objects.title: Waistcoat worn by General George Washington
objects.displayTitle: Waistcoat worn by General George Washington
objects.imageAlt: Photograph of Washington’s Buff Wool Waistcoat
objects.description: Collarless, buff wool waistcoat with a single row of fourteen metal buttons down the front, worn by General George Washington. Waistcoat is lined with linen, and has two front flap pockets, each with four buttons beneath flap. Although presented through the years as a uniform consisting of coat, waistcoat and breeches, the waistcoat and breeches are actually from an earlier uniform dating from the end of the Revolutionary War. The coat is slightly newer, dating from 1789
objects.story: Washington gets dressed for the day. Under his army coat he wears this wool waistcoat, a kind of vest. His outfit has more than one layer!

objects.story: This is not just one book. The museum catalog lists 71 volumes in this Washington book collection.

objects.title: Submarine Lunch Box
objects.imageAlt: Museum image for Submarine Lunch Box
objects.description: This tin lunch box was manufactured by Thermos in 1960. It has a metal snap for a hinged lid and a collapsible, red plastic handle. The art on the lunch box features images of four submarines on the back and sides. The submarines are the USS Nautilus, Seawolf, Skipjack, and George Washington. The George Washington is shown firing an underwater missile, and there is a cross-section of the USS Nautilus on the bottom.
